strengths: Novel self-consistency framework: Theorems 2.1-3.1 elegantly characterize diffusion bridges via a new self-consistency property, with rigorous proofs connecting to the HJB equation (Theorem D.2)
Computational efficiency: Avoids backpropagation through simulated trajectories, achieving ~3× speedup over NGDB (230s vs 800s for OU bridges) while maintaining comparable accuracy
Practical innovation: Creative solution to Jacobian explosion through generalized self-consistency property with auxiliary drift (Theorem B.1), handling challenging settings like potential barriers

Comprehensive theoretical treatment: Detailed mathematical framework including fixed-point loss formulation, online learning algorithm, and multiple variants (standard/generalized, different α-schedules, STL adjustments)

Thorough experimental evaluation: Systematic evaluation on diverse benchmarks (OU, CIR, double-well, cell diffusion, Müller-Brown) with access to ground truth KL divergence, multiple baselines, and ablations
Clear presentation: Well-structured paper with effective illustrations (Figures 1-2), clear algorithms (1-3), and comprehensive appendices with complete proofs
weaknesses: Limited empirical gains over NGDB: Primary advantage is computational cost, not solution quality. OU bridges show comparable accuracy, Müller-Brown results are slightly worse (27.8±1.7 vs 28.6±0.4), and CIR/cell diffusion show negligible differences

Fixed-point loss lacks convergence guarantees: Equation (8-9) presents a pragmatic self-play approximation with double dependency on u, but provides no formal convergence analysis or rate characterization

Problem-dependent tuning required: Method needs careful selection of auxiliary drift b̃ (b̃=0 fails entirely on Müller-Brown), loss clipping values, and α-schedules depending on problem geometry—reducing off-the-shelf applicability

Jacobian explosion mitigation complexity: Standard algorithm with b̃=0 cannot handle challenging settings; practitioners must understand problem geometry to set b̃, adding implementation burden. STL adjustments incur ~1.5× computational overhead

Limited scope and applicability: Restriction to elliptic diffusions (σσ^T full rank) excludes hypoelliptic problems; acknowledged as future work but limits current impact. High variance in some experiments (Table 2: 1.7 vs 0.4)

Incomplete analysis of related work: Self-consistency property also derived independently by Pidstrigach et al. (2025) from Malliavin calculus; paper does not clearly articulate what is novel beyond computational efficiency. Connection to Domingo-Enrich et al. SOC literature relegated to appendix

strengths: Solid theoretical contributions with rigorous proofs. The self-consistency characterization (Theorem 2.1) is elegant and Theorem 3.1 properly establishes uniqueness by combining self-consistency with terminal and gradient-form conditions.
Practical algorithm design that avoids backpropagation through trajectories via fixed-point-style losses, achieving ~3.5× speedup in favorable cases.
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks with thorough ablations (α-schedules, STL adjustments). Experimental details are well-documented for reproducibility.
Clear presentation of core concepts (Figures 1-2) and extensive appendices with detailed proofs and algorithms.
Principled generalization via auxiliary drift (Appendix B.4) to handle Jacobian explosion, demonstrating theoretical depth.
weaknesses: Marginal empirical advantages over NGDB baseline. Most experiments show comparable or slightly worse performance (Table 1): OE comparable KL, double-well degrades with barrier height, Muller-Brown shows higher variance. This undermines the core value proposition.

Computational advantage substantially overstated. While avoiding trajectory backprop provides ~3.5× speedup, STL adjustments (needed for accuracy on hard problems) increase cost by 1.5×, eroding claimed benefits. With STL: speedup largely negated. Without STL: reduced accuracy (Table 4).

Theoretical-practical gap not fully addressed. Appendix B.1 admits gradient form is not theoretically required at all times but necessary in practice to prevent 'rotational term' accumulation. No convergence analysis provided for the fixed-point loss training procedure.

Limited novelty: self-consistency property is acknowledged as derivable from Pidstrigach et al. (2025)'s Malliavin calculus. Core contribution is applying via fixed-point losses—relatively incremental methodologically.

Method brittleness and hyperparameter sensitivity. Performance critically depends on α-schedule: Table 3 shows endpoint schedule causes catastrophic failure (KL=3.49±2.40 vs 0.15 for average) on double-well. No principled guidance for practitioners on schedule selection.

Robustness concerns. Core method fails on challenging Muller-Brown problem (Figure 9a), requiring switch to generalized version with ̃b=-b. Suggests basic form is not robust; need for variants adds complexity and suggests fundamental limitations.

Presentation is dense (26+26 pages) for the focused contribution. Key practical insights relegated to appendices (e.g., when generalized version is necessary). Distinction between standard and generalized versions unclear in main text.

Incomplete analysis of limitations. Ellipticity requirement noted but not discussed. No systematic characterization of success/failure modes. Missing analysis of why KL-based objectives (NGDB) are superior for terminal-time accuracy.
Fixed-point loss convergence unanalyzed. Uses 'self-play' style training with stop-gradient but provides no convergence guarantees or monotonicity analysis for fixed-point iteration.
Practitioners gain little actionable insight. Unclear when to use this method vs. NGDB vs. alternatives. With comparable results and additional tuning requirements, NGDB remains simpler choice.

strengths: Novel self-consistency characterization of diffusion bridges with rigorous theoretical justification (Theorems 2.1 and 3.1); elegant fixed-point property u*(s,x) = E[J^T_t|s u*(t,X_t)|X_s] provides new perspective on the problem
Practical computational advantage: avoids backpropagation through trajectories, achieving 3-4× speedup over NGDB while maintaining comparable accuracy

Comprehensive theoretical development including generalized self-consistency property (Appendix B.4) to handle Jacobian explosion, STL adjustments from HJB equation, and complete characterization via Theorem D.2

Extensive experimental validation across five diverse settings (OU with ground truth, CIR with spatially-dependent σ, double-well rare events, non-conservative cell diffusion, challenging Müller-Brown) with thorough ablations on α-schedules and STL adjustments
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, logical progression, and comprehensive 26-page appendix containing detailed algorithms, proofs, and experimental details

Sound methodology: drift parameterization (Eq. 7) cleverly enforces gradient form and guides toward terminal point; fixed-point training elegantly handles dual dependencies on θ without explicit trajectory backpropagation
Honest treatment of limitations including ellipticity requirements, simulation costs during training, and problem-dependent need for generalized version
weaknesses: Marginal practical improvements over existing methods: performance is predominantly comparable to NGDB (Tables 1, 3, 4) with main advantage being 3-4× speedup; on Müller-Brown, NGDB slightly outperforms (28.6 vs 27.8); improvements often within error bars

Limited scalability: all experiments are low-dimensional (d ≤ 2 primarily); dimension scaling only shown to d=30 with visible performance degradation; no discussion of computational scaling or feasibility in high dimensions where Jacobian computation becomes expensive

Algorithm requires careful problem-specific tuning: standard version fails on Müller-Brown requiring generalized version (b̃=-b); different α-schedules needed for different problems; loss clipping required in some cases, suggesting brittleness

Theoretical approximations in training targets (Eq. 12): second integral approximated by single-step value; fixed-point approach separates dependencies; no convergence analysis or sample complexity bounds; gap between fixed-point optimization and satisfaction of true self-consistency property unexplored

Experimental scope limited to synthetic benchmarks: no real applications demonstrated despite mentioning chemistry, finance, shape evolution; Müller-Brown is harder but still toy example; ground truth only for OU/CIR/double-well, making verification difficult for realistic problems

Technical gaps in theory: Theorem 3.1 enforces gradient form throughout time but Theorem D.2(iv) only requires it at one point—this practical restriction is justified for stability but appears ad-hoc; uniqueness argument in vorticity PDE (Eq. 69) relies on unstated 'standard regularity assumptions'

Limited guidance for practitioners: no clear decision criteria for when to use standard vs. generalized version; sensitivity to auxiliary drift choice b̃ unexplored; choice of α-schedule appears problem-dependent without principled selection method

Presentation: important connection to stochastic optimal control (B.5) relegated to appendix; some key details mentioned only in passing (e.g., loss clipping for Müller-Brown); heavy notation makes sections dense; no discussion of expected failure modes
